title: Stand like an anvil (Ignatius to Polycarp 3)
hookLine: Ignatius tells Bishop Polycarp: stand firm like an anvil being struck
tomorrow: an old man in a loud stadium is told to curse Christ. his answer?

cards: The phone buzzes again. Same person, same argument, round four. The pull is to fire back something sharp, or to block them and vanish.
There's a third picture, and it comes from a blacksmith's shop. The hammer comes down, sparks fly, the hot iron bends into shape. And the anvil underneath doesn't move.
It doesn't hit back. It doesn't walk away. One bishop sent that picture to another, in a short letter that's still read.

teach.b: The letter is from Ignatius, a bishop who, tradition says, wrote while being taken to Rome under guard. He writes to Polycarp, bishop of the church in Smyrna. Chapter three opens on pressure.
People will come who seem believable but teach strange things, he says. Don't let them shake you.
Stand firm, like an anvil being struck. It's the mark of a great athlete to take the blows and still win.
That's one voice, and it has company: Paul tells the Corinthians, "stand fast in the faith," and Ephesians says, "having done all, to stand." Its best case: steadiness is the strength.
The blows land, the real work goes on, and time shows who was right. But there's a second voice in the same scriptures.
Paul tells the Galatians about a clash with Peter in Antioch: "I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed."

teach.h: TWO WAYS OF NOT BEING MOVED.
teach.b: Its best case: sometimes standing firm means opening your mouth, a clear word, face to face, before a wrong spreads. Christians have leaned on both. Ignatius himself didn't stay quiet; he wrote letters.
And Paul, who spoke up, also wrote "stand fast." The anvil and the face-to-face word are both ways of not being moved.

how: Christians read Ignatius's letters for courage under pressure, and churches that remember him keep a feast day in his name.

games.q: what does “stand like an anvil” mean?
o: refusing to change a single thing, ever
staying firm under blows without striking back
hitting back twice as hard as you were hit

games.q: the anvil letter — tap the pairs.
p: wrote: stand like a struck anvil
bishop of Smyrna, the letter's reader
takes the blows and still wins

s: standing firm, in Ignatius's picture, means hitting back hard
the anvil takes the blows; it doesn't swing back or walk away.
Paul says he withstood Peter to his face
Galatians 2:11: because he was to be blamed.
Ignatius wrote this letter to Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna
the anvil line comes in chapter 3.

games.q: your coach keeps cracking jokes about your faith in front of the team. one teammate says: let it bounce off, like Ignatius's anvil. another says: Paul withstood Peter to his face, so say something. what's the best case for speaking up?
o: a calm, direct word, face to face, can be part of standing firm.
speaking up proves you have no patience at all.
anvils never move, so silence is always required.
games.why: Paul says he withstood Peter to the face; Ignatius says stand like a struck anvil. Christians lean on both: steadiness that won't swing back, and a clear word that won't hide.

practice: Stand, if you can, and feel your feet on the floor; if standing isn't possible, feel your weight settle into the chair.
Bring to mind one pressure leaning on you now, and don't fight it or fix it: stay planted, like the anvil, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Stand like an anvil. Ignatius's word to Polycarp: stay firm under the blows, the way an anvil stays under the hammer.

orig.note: Greek: anvil. Ignatius uses it in his letter to Polycarp, chapter 3.

carryVoice: Your line: stand like an anvil. The blows land, and the anvil stays. Hold steady.
